prize_parts.citation: For a visionary Romanian-language oeuvre, grounded in poetry and carried into large prose cycles, that builds memory, the body and dream into a sustained metaphysical architecture.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: one prize part, B014, with the single credited name Mircea Cărtărescu. Round 1 produced no new evidence that moves the literary case, and it did not weaken it. On the common criteria, the voice is distinctive, and the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid are conceived as large, patterned structures in which memory, the body and dream-logic form one project. The supplied descriptions and public knowledge place poetry at the base of the prose, which supports a whole-oeuvre reading rather than a single-book reading. Attribution is unambiguous. All six round-1 files prefer B014, and I do not count that as merit. The chair's questions test it better than a count would, and the case holds under them for three reasons. First, the architecture is visible even through translation, so my confidence rests on something I can state without relying on reputation. Second, the translation caveat applies equally to Can Xue and Adonis, so it does not favour one candidate over another. Third, no colleague offered a concrete reason to think the later volumes only repeat the earlier ones. That is an absence of evidence, not proof. One thing did change: the citation wording. The chair noted that the poetic strand is the thinnest in translation. I therefore now say the oeuvre is 'grounded in poetry and carried into large prose cycles', not that it is an oeuvre of poetry and prose in equal measure. This keeps the poetic origin that colleagues describe and does not claim more for the poetry than the evidence supports.
statement.case_against: The reservation I cannot remove is that the claim depends on Romanian sentence rhythm and density, which I can judge only through translations of uneven quality. I cannot confirm volume by volume that the later work extends the project rather than recirculating its motifs. Poetry and early work are thinly visible to me, so the 'grounded in poetry' part of the citation is the least secure part of it. Olsson raised a further check I take seriously: a metaphysical, inward project can be overvalued by readers drawn to it, and unanimity among six readers with the same translated corpus may reflect shared limits of reading as much as shared judgment. I have not independently verified any source. If the committee's reading showed the late novels repeating earlier devices without new formal solutions, or showed the poetry to be minor, I would reconsider my preference and the citation scope. Nothing in the exchange shows that at present.

responses.point: Olsson conceded that Can Xue's case is stronger than his eighth-place opening ranking implied, but still wants evidence of development within her work, for example how later novels differ in kind from early stories, before placing her above Cărtărescu. He also asks the committee to press whether he overvalues a metaphysical, inward project.
responses.response: I welcome the move on Can Xue. It narrows our disagreement to evidence of development, not to whether her voice is real. I agree that is the right test, and I cannot meet it from the supplied material, which lists Frontier and Love in the New Millennium and little more. I would hold that same test against Cărtărescu rather than assume his arc is established. The difference for me is that his development is partly visible in the form of the large works, whereas for her I would need examples of change across decades. On your wider caution, I think the useful check is whether the case can be stated through the sentence and the formal solution, not through the cosmology as theme. I believe it can, but only partly, because I read the sentence in translation. So I hold the preference with that qualification and have not strengthened it.

responses.point: Carlberg takes Can Xue's claim more seriously after round 1. She still holds that the unity of her oeuvre is harder to state in a citation than Cărtărescu's, because her method works through repeated estrangement in shorter pieces while his builds across large forms. She also argues that the translation limitation should be applied evenly to Cărtărescu, Can Xue and Adonis.
responses.response: I agree with the evenness principle, and it makes me restate my own reasoning. Cărtărescu is also read by us in translation. So the asymmetry between him and Can Xue is not that his prose survives translation and hers does not. It is that his large-scale structure is visible in the works I can name, and her development is not visible to me yet. I cannot confirm from the supplied material that her output is mostly shorter pieces, and her work may well include longer forms. That is itself something to test before it is used against her citation. Separately, I must correct my round-1 response to you. I attributed to you a concern that Carson's later work may be uneven, and the chair has noted that it is not in your file. I withdraw that attribution. The concern about Carson's scale and citation scope is my own question, and Palm raised related points. I have not verified the full bibliography, so I should not claim unevenness either.

responses.point: Palm leans toward reading recurrence in the Cărtărescu cycles as an architectural principle rather than mere accumulation, but calls that a judgment rather than a verified fact. She ranked Carson sixth because the best-known work is compact and part of the oeuvre is scholarly or translation work that sits uneasily in a citation.
responses.response: I accept that distinction and think it can be tested: recurrence is architectural if later volumes alter the formal solution they inherit, and accumulation if they only add. I cannot show that from public summaries, so I share your caution about calling it a fact. On Carson, I concede that compact scale and the weight of the scholarly and translation components bear on citation scope. My position remains that inventiveness and intellectual depth, not volume, are what a whole-oeuvre criterion should weigh. But I also accept that a citation must say what the whole is, and for her that is harder to state than for Cărtărescu. That is why she remains a second alternative behind Can Xue and not my lead. I do not treat the hybrid form as a barrier. The unresolved matter is scope.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg keeps Can Xue as the leading alternative on originality of voice and argues that translation limits are the committee's own reading problem, not a reason to discount her. He ranks Marie NDiaye third and says the case rests on controlled estrangement in the sentence.
responses.response: I agree that distinctiveness of voice deserves real weight and that translation limits should not be turned into a penalty against her alone. That is why she is my first alternative. On NDiaye I ranked her sixth, so I do not dismiss her. I read the control of estrangement as real, but I share Palm's and your own doubt about scale, and I cannot say whether the uncanny method keeps deepening across novels and plays. For me that places her below Can Xue as an alternative. It is a judgment about the evidence available to me, not a verdict on the oeuvre. If you can point to a work where the method changes in kind, that would move me.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Can Xue below Cărtărescu because his cycles are cumulative in scale and register, and she adds that part of Can Xue's strangeness may be a translation effect that neither of us can settle. She keeps Can Xue as her first alternative because the voice is unmistakable and the radicalism sustained.
responses.response: We are in close agreement. I would sharpen one point after reading Carlberg's evenness argument. If strangeness in Can Xue may be a translation effect, then some of the density we admire in Cărtărescu may also be shaped by his translators. I therefore do not rest the ranking on a claim that his prose translates better. I rest it on the more visible evidence of cumulative structure and of a poetry-to-prose arc, while admitting that the poetry is the thinner part. In answer to the chair's question on Adonis, my not placing him in my top eight reflects my inability to assess Arabic prosody through translation. It is not a literary reservation, and I do not want it read as one.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's achievement depends on Romanian sentence rhythm and density, and how faithful the translations of the large novels are. I judge this only through translation.

Whether the poetry and early work, thinly visible in translation, justify the 'grounded in poetry' clause of the citation, and whether late volumes extend or only repeat the project. I cannot settle this volume by volume from public summaries.
How much of Can Xue's output exists in translation, and whether her method deepens across decades or repeats. The translation caveat applies to her and to Cărtărescu alike.
How a citation for Carson's hybrid scholarly, lyric and translation practice would be framed within the will's reference to literary work, and whether its scope is manageable.
Adonis's claimed prosodic achievement in Arabic is outside what I can assess. I have not independently verified any source or read any work in the original language.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to any shortlisted writer is apparent from the supplied profile. My own work as a novelist and my joining the committee in 2021 together with Ellen Mattson are context only, not candidate-related ties and not evidence of preference. Disclosure update: in round 1 I attributed to Carlberg a concern about Carson's later work that is not in her file, and I have withdrawn that attribution above. This is a citation error, not a conflict of interest. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated.
